speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. You have a significant medical history along with gait and limb ataxia; to begin our evaluation, could you describe the specific nature of your ataxia and when your symptoms first started? Additionally, what are the major components of your past medical history?

speaker: Patient
text: I started having trouble walking recently, and people say I look drunk when I walk. I also feel clumsy in my arms and legs, especially on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text: The symptoms you describe sound concerning; could you clarify if your right-sided clumsiness is worse when you close your eyes in the dark, and have you noticed any issues with your sense of vibration or position in your feet? Also, given your significant medical history, are you currently on any specific medications or have you had recent changes in your health?

speaker: Patient
text: I have Crohn disease and it has been difficult to control. I have been taking natalizumab for about a year. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Multiple Sclerosis with Crohn's disease. The combination of a confirmed Crohn's diagnosis and a prior clinical suspicion of MS by another physician strongly points to MS, but the atypical response to natalizumab (which is used for MS, not Crohn's) suggests an alternative diagnosis such as Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) or MOG antibody disease, potentially complicated by medication-induced neuropathy or misdiagnosis. Immediate testing for Aquaporin-4 and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies is necessary to confirm or rule out NMOSD/MOG-AD, given the patient's history and current treatment failure.

REQUEST TEST: Aquaporin_4 Antibodies, MOG Antibodies, and MRI of Brain and Spine with contrast.
